Adult Carolines parrotfish regularly attain a body length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] when fully grown, a measurement derived from field surveys conducted across the Hawaiian Archipelago. This ultimate size is achieved after a prolonged growth phase, with individuals following a length-weight relationship characteristic of the Scaridae family. In terms of reproductive development, the onset of gonadal maturation occurs when individuals reach a total length of 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters], a size threshold that typically corresponds to the initiation of sexual differentiation in this protogynous hermaphrodite. At this length, the estimated wet weight at puberty is 347.4 g [Wwp = 347.4 g]rams, reflecting the substantial somatic investment required before reproductive tissues begin to develop. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical allometric scaling pattern, with the body mass increasing disproportionally as the fish grow larger. These life-history traits position Calotomus carolinus as a moderately large-bodied parrotfish, comparable in asymptotic size to several other scraping excavators within the tribe Scarini.

Newly hatched larvae of Carolines parrotfish emerge from the egg at an extraordinarily small size, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.00023 g [Wwb = 0.00023 g]rams. This minuscule initial mass is characteristic of pelagic-spawning teleosts, where the yolksac larva must rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days after eclosion. The diameter of the ovum, estimated at approximately 0.75 millimeters based on observations in related chaetodontid species, dictates the limited space available for yolk storage within the chorionated egg. Following a brief endotrophic phase lasting several days, the prolarva undergoes yolk-sac resorption and commences first exogenous feeding, marking the transition to an actively growing pelagic larval phase. During this early period, mortality is exceptionally high, a common feature among reef fishes that produce numerous small offspring. The extreme fecundity associated with such a diminutive birth mass is an evolutionary strategy that compensates for the negligible survival probability of individual larvae during their planktonic dispersal stage.

Where water temperatures average 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Caroline's parrotfish has been estimated at approximately 12% [GSI = approximately 12%]. This value, extrapolated from studies on the congeneric Hipposcarus longiceps, reflects a reproductive strategy involving three distinct spawning events per year, a pattern common among iteroparous scarids that broadcast their gametes during seasonal aggregations. At this temperature, metabolic rates are elevated, supporting the energetic demands of both somatic maintenance and gamete production. Field observations suggest that spawning activity in Calotomus carolinus coincides with lunar cycles, with peak gamete release occurring around the full moon phase, thereby synchronizing larval release with favorable oceanographic conditions for dispersal.

The maximum longevity recorded for Carolines parrotfish in their natural habitat spans 13 years [am = 13 years], a lifespan determined through mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith increment analysis at a mean annual water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This duration, which corresponds to approximately 4745 days of life, positions the species as moderately long-lived among the smaller-bodied scarids, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances repeated reproductive bouts against the cumulative risks of predation and senescence. The attainment of this ultimate mass coincides with a plateau in the growth curve, after which further increases in body size are negligible. Growth trajectories derived from length-frequency distributions indicate that the majority of somatic expansion occurs during the first five to seven years, with subsequent years devoted primarily to reproductive output rather than continued mass accumulation.

Comparisons with other parrotfishes reveal that Calotomus carolinus occupies an intermediate position along the life-history continuum, with its adult body mass of 1600 g [Wwi = 1600 g]rams representing a substantial investment in somatic tissue that supports both foraging efficiency and predator avoidance on complex coral reef substrates. The length-based metrics for this species, with a total length at puberty of 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters] and an ultimate length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], demonstrate a clear separation between the size at first reproduction and the asymptotic size, a pattern that allows for continued somatic growth alongside reproductive activity. These parameters collectively describe a species that has evolved a bet-hedging strategy in the variable and resource-limited environment of Indo-Pacific coral reefs.
